frames.title: Let camera choices express story intent
frames.summary: Framing, movement, and exposure should translate emotional and narrative priorities into visual behavior.
principles: Choose the camera relationship that best reflects audience alignment.
Movement should reveal, pursue, or pressure something specific.
Protect spatial clarity before adding flourish.
Visual style should evolve with the story's changing emotional temperature.
patterns: Use repeated camera grammar to establish a scene's rules before breaking them.
Tie lensing and movement to point of view shifts.
antiPatterns: Do not move the camera just to announce production value.
Do not sacrifice geography for momentary coolness.

frames.title: Pick lenses for felt perspective
frames.summary: Lens choice affects intimacy, distortion, depth, and how a space emotionally reads.
principles: Wider lenses emphasize environment, proximity, and movement through space.
Longer lenses compress distance and isolate subjects through selective focus.
Changing focal length should reflect a storytelling reason, not indecision.
Lens consistency can unify a sequence's emotional texture.
patterns: Use wider focal lengths when environment pressure is part of the beat.
Use longer focal lengths to flatten choice or trap attention.
antiPatterns: Do not treat lenses as neutral coverage tools.
Do not mix incompatible lens logic without a visible point.

frames.title: Direct attention with deliberate composition
frames.summary: Composition should clarify what matters, how power flows, and what emotional tension lives in the frame.
principles: Use balance, imbalance, and negative space to shape feeling.
Foreground, midground, and background should support readable depth of meaning.
Lines and blocking should guide the eye toward story information.
Change composition when power or perspective changes.
patterns: Reserve centered symmetry for ritual, control, or destabilizing contrast.
Use occlusion when hiding is part of the tension.
antiPatterns: Do not decorate the frame until the focal idea is clear.
Do not overfill every edge of the image.

frames.title: Stage relationships through movement and distance
frames.summary: Blocking makes status, attraction, conflict, and attention legible before a line is spoken.
principles: Assign each movement a change in intention, status, or knowledge.
Use proximity and eye line to expose relationship dynamics.
Let performers discover beats through action, not marks alone.
Coordinate blocking with lensing so the audience reads the intended power shift.
patterns: Crossing frame lines can signify challenge or takeover when motivated.
Use stillness as an active choice against surrounding motion.
antiPatterns: Do not make actors wander without dramatic consequence.
Do not ignore the room's practical pathways and obstacles.
